podcast.body: Chosen by Elvis for his first RCA session, this song was initially conceived by Tommy Durden (inspired by a newspaper story about a man, possibly Alvin Crowley, who died by suicide or was shot during a robbery), with Mae Axton contributing the iconic "heartbreak hotel" phrase. Glenn Reeves helped finish it and recorded the demo but refused credit. Elvis instantly loved the song, which reminded him of Roy Brown's "Hard-Luck Blues," and Mae Axton insisted it would be his first million-seller. Despite criticisms about its reverb sound compared to Sun Records' slapback, it became a smash hit, reaching number one on the Pop and Country charts and the top five in R&B, marking his transformation into "the King of Rock and Roll." "He instantly fell in love with the song, which reminded the young blues lover of Roy Brown's hard-look blues."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.body: This significant Elvis Presley hit from 1956, along with "Hound Dog," achieved considerable success, but its global chart performance was ultimately outdone by Fats Domino's "Blueberry Hill" in the same year. "Worldwide, Blueberry Hill was the biggest rock and roll hit of 1956, outdoing even Elvis's Hound Dog and Hard Break Hotel in Worldwide Chart positions."

podcast.body: This song marked Elvis Presley's first single release for RCA. It competed on the charts directly with Carl Perkins's "Blue Suede Shoes," with "Heartbreak Hotel" ultimately reaching number one and "Blue Suede Shoes" peaking at number two. Both singles were significant cross-over hits, achieving top two positions on both Pop and Country charts, and top five in R&B. "Heartbreak Hotel ended up at number one, and Blue Sway Chuse at number two, and both were cross-over-hit, making the top two in both Pop and Country, and the top five in R&B."
